newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan says U.S. official mistaken on air talks.
newsitem.headline: Japan says U.S. official mistaken on air talks.

text.p: Japan's Transport Ministry on Friday denied it had linked the issue of the safety of a U.S. airline to bilateral aviation talks.
A ministry official said senior White House official Daniel Tarullo was "mistaken" in making the accusation.
"He's mistaken. Discussions about the individual airlines were not a part of the latest round of air talks," the official said.
He added that safety and air talks were separate issues handled by different sections of the ministry.

Tarullo, who is assistant to President Bill Clinton for international economics, said on Thursday that Japan's request that the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) look at Northwest Airlines Corp maintenance operations was a scare tactic aimed at gaining a negotiating advantage.
In March, Japan asked the FAA to investigate Northwest's maintenance operations as the company had shown an unusual number of "irregular flight operations".
The ministry said that 20 of 51 incidents in 1996 at Narita airport outside Tokyo involved Northwest and that the airline's rate was double the average.
Another ministry official said the FAA had looked at Northwest's maintenance operations at Narita.

The FAA said there were no safety problems but recommended that the company set up an internal committee to look into the high number of incidents, he said, adding that the ministry was waiting for a report from the company.
Officials from Japan and the United States have been meeting over the past year to try to resolve problems in their current air pact and to set the stage for talks on a more liberal accord.
